about: Xquic, carrying the unborn twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque, comes to the house of the grandmother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen (the text calls her their mother) and greets her as her daughter-in-law. The old woman will not have her: where are her sons? did they not die in Xibalba? Hunbatz and Hunchouen are all that is left of them. Xquic answers that Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu are not dead, and that the old woman will see their face in the children she carries. Hunbatz and Hunchouen, meanwhile, spend their days at the flute and song, at painting and carving, and are their grandmother's comfort. The grandmother calls Xquic a wanton and a deceiver, then sets her a test: if she is truly her daughter-in-law, let her bring back a great net full of food from the maize field of Hunbatz and Hunchouen. In the field there is only a single plant. Xquic despairs, then calls on the Guardian of Food and on Xtoh, Xcanil and Xcacau; she draws on the silk of the one ear, the net fills with ears of maize, and animals carry it home for her. The grandmother goes to the field, finds the single plant still standing and the place where the net lay at its foot, hurries home, and takes it as the sign that Xquic is truly her daughter-in-law.

sentences.t: Arecut e ꜭo ri vchuch Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, ta xul ri ixoc Xquic vbi.
sentences.l: This-then they there-are the his-mother Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, when she-arrived the woman Xquic her-name.
sentences.i: Now they were there, the mother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen, when the woman called Xquic arrived.
sentences.n: Ximénez's indented paragraph, the only one in this stretch: the story turns from Xibalba back to the house of Hunhunahpu. Arecut 'this then' (are 'this is' + cut 'then' written as one word). e ꜭo 'they are there': e is the plural, so the household seems meant, the old woman with the two boys (inferred; Brasseur 'était chez elle'); ꜭo 'there is, be there' (MS egori, the g-shaped letter read ꜭ). vchuch Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen 'the mother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen': v- 'his, her' + chuch 'mother', with the owner named after the noun. The woman meant is Xmucane, who is their grandmother: their own mother died in 009, and in 010 Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, leaving for Xibalba, told the two to keep 'your grandmother' warm. Brasseur's note says the same: 'La mère apparemment pour l'aïeule'. The English follows the manuscript. In Hunchouen the middle letter is v-shaped here; it is printed u, as in 009–012. xul 'she arrived': x- (completed action) + ul 'arrive here'. ixoc 'woman'. Xquic is the maiden of the last part (toggle Xkik').

sentences.t: Ta xul cut ri ixoc Xquic ruꜭ ri vchuch Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen;
sentences.l: When she-arrived then the woman Xquic with-her the his-mother Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen;
sentences.i: the woman Xquic came to the mother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen;
sentences.n: The arrival is told a second time, now with where she came: ruꜭ 'with her, to her' (r- 'her' + uꜭ 'company'; MS rug, read ꜭ). Brasseur's text runs from the first ixok Xquiq straight on to ruq ri u chuch, leaving out vbi. Ta xul cut ri ixoc Xquic; the manuscript has both clauses, and both are printed.

sentences.t: xꜭol oc ral chupam, xa zcaquin chic maui que yaqueic ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque qui bi.
sentences.l: it-lay(?) already her-child inside-her, only a-little now not they come-forth(?) the Hunahpu, Xbalanque their-name.
sentences.i: Her child was already within her, and it was only a little while before those called Hunahpu and Xbalanque would come forth (?).
sentences.n: xꜭol oc is one word in the manuscript (xgoloc), divided with Brasseur's x-qol-oc: x- + ꜭol, taken as the form of ꜭo 'be there' that says where a thing lies (inferred), + oc 'already', as in 009's xcaminac oc. ral chupam 'her child within her': ral, r- 'her' + al, a woman's child (Ximénez writes rall; his final ll on this page is printed l, as earlier parts print ral, val, lal). xa zcaquin chic maui 'only a little more, and not yet' is the phrase of 007 and 008 ('within a little'). que yaqueic: que is c- + e 'they'; yaqueic was taken in 009 as 'bearing, ways' (a guess); here it must say something like 'come forth, be born', after Brasseur's 'peu s'en fallait pour la naissance de ceux qui se nommèrent Hunahpu et Xbalanqué' (a guess; toggle yakeik, as in 009). Hunahpu and Xbalanque are the two boys of 003–008, here not yet born.

sentences.t: Ta xul curi ixoc chire ri atit; xꜭha curi ixoc chire ri atit: “Mi xin vlic, lal chichu; in alib la, in puch alcual la, lal chichu,” xꜭha, ta xoc vloc ruꜭ ri atit.
sentences.l: When she-arrived then-the woman to-her the grandmother; she-said then-the woman to-her the grandmother: “Just-now I arrived-here, you(lady) mother(?); I daughter-in-law your(lady), I also child your(lady), you(lady) mother(?),” she-said, when she-entered hither with-her the grandmother.
sentences.i: So the woman came to the grandmother, and the woman said to the grandmother: “I have come, lady mother; I am your daughter-in-law, I am your child, lady mother,” she said, as she came in to the grandmother.
sentences.n: Two parallel lines bring her in: xul … chire ri atit, xꜭha … chire ri atit 'she came to the grandmother, she said to the grandmother'. curi 'then' (cu + ri). atit is 'grandmother' and also 'old woman' (Ratit Ꜫih, Ratit Zac in the first part; ivatit 'your grandmother' in 010). Mi xin vlic 'I have just arrived': mi 'just now' + x- + in 'I' + vlic 'arrive here'. lal is the respectful 'you' (as in lal ahau 'my lord'); chichu is taken as a respectful word for an older woman, 'lady, mother', after Brasseur's 'ó ma dame et mère' and chuch 'mother' (inferred; toggle by the letters). alib is the in-law word: here 'daughter-in-law' (Brasseur 'votre belle-fille'), but in ¶4 Xquic calls the grandmother valib too, so the word seems to name the tie from both sides (inferred). la after it is the respectful 'your'. alcual 'child, children' is al (a woman's child) + ꜭahol (a man's son) made one word, as in 009's ralcualah (toggle alk'wal); Brasseur 'la fille adoptive de votre seigneurie'. The speech opens and closes with lal chichu. xoc vloc 'she came in': xoc 'entered' + vloc 'hither'.

sentences.t: “Apa cat pe vi vloc? Ꜭo chi pa ri val? Ma pa xe camic chi Xibalba?
sentences.l: “Where you come there hither? There-is still (pa) the my-child? Not (pa) they-died at Xibalba?
sentences.i: “Where have you come from? Is there still a child of mine? Did they not die in Xibalba?
sentences.n: The grandmother answers with questions. Apa … vi 'where … from': apa asks the place and vi points back to it; cat 'you (one)', c- (ongoing) + at 'you'; pe 'come'; vloc 'hither'. Ꜭo chi pa ri val 'is there still my child?': ꜭo chi as in the ꜭo chi vi 'is there any more' of an earlier part, chi standing for chic 'still, any more' (toggle chik); pa marks the question (Brasseur prints qo, the g-shaped letter read ꜭ). val 'my child': v- 'my' before a vowel + al (MS vall). She means her sons, Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu (Brasseur 'où sont mes fils?'). Ma pa … 'is it not that …?'. xe camic 'they died': xe- (they, completed) + cam 'die' + -ic. chi Xibalba 'at Xibalba'.

sentences.t: E cu caib canoc quetal, qui ꜩihel puch, Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen qui bi; ve a vila? Cat pe vi, cat el vbic!” xuꜭhax ri capoh rumal atit.
sentences.l: They then two left-behind their-sign, their-word also, Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen their-name; if you-see-them? You come there, you go-out thither!” she-was-told the maiden by grandmother.
sentences.i: Two are left behind, their sign and their word, Hunbatz and Hunchouen by name; do you see them? Go back where you came from (?); out, away with you!” the maiden was told by the grandmother.
sentences.n: E cu caib canoc 'they, then, two, left behind': e the plural, caib 'two', canoc 'left behind' (canah 'remain' + -oc). quetal, qui ꜩihel puch is a pair: quetal is qu- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + etal 'sign, trace' (vetal in an earlier part, where etal can also mean 'descendants'); ꜩihel is ꜩih 'word' + -el, 'their word' (inferred; toggle ki tzijel). The sons left behind are the sign and the word of their dead fathers; Brasseur 'leurs deux descendants, les signes de leur parole'. ve a vila (MS ve avila, divided by us; Brasseur's OCR is garbled here): ve 'if, whether' + a v-, the 'your, you' a- with v before a vowel (written apart here), + il 'see' + -a, 'whether you see them' (inferred; Brasseur's French 'ne les vois-tu donc pas?'). Cat pe vi, cat el vbic is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has catpevi, then a small z-shaped mark raised after vi (taken as a pause mark, not a letter), then catelvbic, divided with Brasseur's el ubic. cat 'you (one)', pe 'come', el 'go out', vbic 'thither, away'; the sense 'go back, get out' follows Brasseur ('Sors d'ici, va-t'en!'), inferred. xuꜭhax 'she was told': the passive of ꜭha 'say'. capoh 'maiden' (toggle q'apoj, as in the last parts).

sentences.t: “Xere la, quiꜩih vi chi in alib la; xꜭo nare. In ꜭo vi rech Hunhunahpu.
sentences.l: “So you(lady), truly there that I daughter-in-law your(lady); x-ꜭo(?) nare(?). I there-am there his Hunhunahpu.
sentences.i: “It is so, lady: truly I am your daughter-in-law. I belong to Hunhunahpu.
sentences.n: Xquic answers. Xere la 'just so, lady': xere 'so, this is how', la the respectful particle (MS xerela, one word; Brasseur Xerela). quiꜩih vi chi in alib la 'truly it is that I am your daughter-in-law': quiꜩih 'truly' (ꜩih 'word'). xꜭo nare is a doubtful division (MS … in alibla xgo nare; Brasseur x-qo nare): xꜭo may be x- + ꜭo 'there is', and nare is not understood (in 006 it was left unexplained), so the two words are left out of the English. Brasseur's French has 'Croyez-moi véritablement, je suis certainement votre belle-fille'. In ꜭo vi rech Hunhunahpu 'I am his, Hunhunahpu's': ꜭo 'be there' (Brasseur qo), rech 'of him, his' (r- + ech); Brasseur supplies '(l'épouse)'. The manuscript writes the name apart here (hunhun ahpu), and hun hunahpu in the next sentence; printed Hunhunahpu, as everywhere. Hunhunahpu is the father of the unborn twins, whose head spoke to her in the last part.

sentences.t: Va vcaam e ꜭazlic; maui e caminac ri Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu; xa vcatbal rib zac mi xqui bano.
sentences.l: This its-carried(?) they alive; not they dead the Hunhunahpu, Vvcub Hunahpu; only its-catbal(?) itself clear(?) just-now they-made.
sentences.i: Here they are, carried, and alive: Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu are not dead; all they have done is make their own sentence (?) shine (?).
sentences.n: Va vcaam e ꜭazlic 'this, the carried, they are alive': vcaam is taken as in 005, v- + caam 'carried' (from cam 'take, carry', with the vowel written double; inferred), here what Xquic carries in her womb; e ꜭazlic 'they are living' (MS egaz|lic, the g-shaped letter read ꜭ; Brasseur qazlic), ꜭazlic of one root with ꜭazlem 'life'. Brasseur 'les voici portés vivants'. maui e caminac 'they are not dead': caminac, cam 'die' + -inac, the state that results. The fathers live on in the unborn sons. xa vcatbal rib zac mi xqui bano is hard: vcatbal (MS plain c; Brasseur u gatbal, his g standing for ꜫ) is not otherwise known; with Brasseur's letter it would be ꜫat 'cut, judge' + -bal, 'judgment' (inferred). rib 'itself, themselves'; zac 'white, clear'; mi xqui bano 'they have just made it'. Brasseur renders 'la sentence qui les a frappés ne les a rendus que plus illustres'. The English is a guess along his lines, and the toggle respells the letters (ukatb'al).

sentences.t: Lal valib. Quehe cut i vila ta chi loc vvach ri vcaam,” xuꜭhaxic ri atit.
sentences.l: You(lady) my-in-law. Thus then you(pl.)-see-it then that dear(?) its-face the its-carried,” she-was-told the grandmother.
sentences.i: You are my mother-in-law. So you shall see the dear (?) face of what is carried,” the grandmother was told.
sentences.n: Lal valib 'you (are) my alib': v- 'my' + alib, the word Xquic used of herself in ¶2. Brasseur renders it here 'Vous êtes ma belle-mère', while the grandmother uses it of Xquic in ¶6, ¶7 and ¶14 ('ma belle-fille'), so alib is taken as the word for the tie between a woman and her son's wife, said from either side (inferred). i vila 'you see it' (MS ivila; Brasseur yv'ila): i- 'you (pl.)', with v before the vowel, + il 'see' + -a; Xquic speaks to the old woman in the plural, out of respect (inferred). ta chi loc: loc has plain c in the manuscript (Brasseur chi log, his g standing for ꜫ) and is taken as 'dear, precious' after his 'leur image chérie', not the loc 'aimlessly' of 003 (inferred; the toggle respells the letters, lok). vvach 'its face', here the likeness of the fathers in the children. xuꜭhaxic 'she was told', with -ic at the end of the sentence.

sentences.t: Arecut que cacal ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen: xa zu, xa bix ca qui bano, xa zibanic, xa pu cotonic qui chaquih chi hutaquih;
sentences.l: This-then they angry(?) the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen: only flute, only song they-do-it, only painting, only also carving their chaquih(?) at each-day;
sentences.i: And Hunbatz and Hunchouen were angry (?): they did nothing but play the flute and sing, nothing but paint and carve; at that they spent (?) every day,
sentences.n: que cacal: que is c- + e 'they'; cacal is not otherwise known (a letter is written over its final l, or it is a blot; read with Brasseur's cakal), and 'angry' is his ('se mirent en colère'), a guess; the toggle respells the letters. The list is the crafts of 009 (ahzu 'flute player', ahbix 'singer', ahꜩibenai 'painter, writer', ahcot 'carver'), now as what they do: zu 'flute', bix 'song', ca qui bano 'they do it' (ca, the ongoing c- written apart; qui- 'they'); zibanic 'painting, writing' (MS plain z, with no ascender, compared with the ꜩ of qui ꜩihel above; Brasseur tzibanic; the toggle respells the letter, sib'anik, as for the plain z of 012's vzibel); cotonic 'carving' (MS plain c; Brasseur qotonic; toggle kotonik, as 009's ahcot ajkot). qui chaquih: chaquih is 'dry', used as a verb in the last part; here Brasseur has 'ils employaient tout le jour', and 'they spent (the day)' is a guess. hutaquih 'every day': hutac 'each' + ꜫih 'day' written as one word, the c and the ꜫ run together (Brasseur hutagih, his g standing for ꜫ; toggle jutaq'ij).

sentences.t: arecut cubul vi vꜭux ri atit.
sentences.l: this-then seated there her-heart the grandmother.
sentences.i: in them the grandmother's heart was at rest.
sentences.n: cubul 'seated, at rest': cub 'sit' + -ul, the ending of a position (inferred; compare cube 'settle' in 004). arecut … vi 'in this … there' points back to the two brothers. vꜭux 'her heart' (MS qux with the q-shaped letter, read ꜭ as in 009). Brasseur: 'ils étaient la consolation de la vieille'. In 010 the two had been charged to keep their grandmother's heart warm.

sentences.t: Xꜭha chicut atit: “Xma ca uah vi at ta valib; xa a hoxbal ri ꜭo cha pam; at ꜭaxtoꜭ. Xe cam vi val ca biyh.”
sentences.l: She-said again-then grandmother: “Not I-want there you (ta) my-daughter-in-law; only your-fornication the there-is in-your belly; you deceiver. They-died there my-child you-tell.”
sentences.i: Then the grandmother said: “I do not want you for my daughter-in-law; what is in your womb is only your wantonness; you are a deceiver. They are dead, my children you speak of.”
sentences.n: Xꜭha chicut 'she said again then' (chic + cut, the c shared). Xma … ta 'not': xma, the negative (elsewhere 'there was not', as xma ꜭo in ¶9), with ta after what is denied. ca uah 'I want' (MS xmacauahvi; Brasseur ca v'ah): ca, the ongoing c- with its vowel, + v- 'I' before a vowel, written u here, + ah 'want' (inferred; toggle waj). at ta valib 'you as my daughter-in-law'. a hoxbal 'your fornication': hox 'lie with' + -bal, as vhoxbal and nu hoxbal in the last part (inferred; Brasseur 'c'est ton adultère'). ri ꜭo cha pam 'which is in your belly' (MS rigo chapam, divided as the last part's co cha pam): cha is chi 'in' + a- 'your'. ꜭaxtoꜭ (MS gaxtog, both letters g-shaped at 3×) is the word used of the boys and of Zipacna in 005–007, 'demon', the colonial word for the devil; said of a woman it is taken as 'deceiver' (inferred; Brasseur's OCR is unreadable here in both his K'iche' and his French). Xe cam vi val 'they are dead, my children': a blot covers vi, read with Brasseur (x-e Cam vi v'al). ca biyh 'you tell of': c- + a- 'you' + biyh 'say, tell' (inferred).

sentences.t: Xꜭha chicut ri atit: “Quiꜩih ibare va ca nu biyh. Vꜩ bala, at valib ca nu tao.
sentences.l: She-said again-then the grandmother: “Truly ibare(?) this I-say. Good bala, you my-daughter-in-law I-hear-it.
sentences.i: And the grandmother said again: “What I say is true. Very well: you are my daughter-in-law, so I hear.
sentences.n: This tag stands at the start of a manuscript line, after ca biyh ends the line before; it is set as the opening of the grandmother's second speech, which runs on to xuꜭhax cut ri capoh 'the maiden was told'. Quiꜩih ibare va ca nu biyh 'truly … this that I say': ibare is not otherwise known and is left out of the English (Brasseur 'Ce n'est que trop vrai tout ce que je t'ai dit'); ca nu biyh 'I say', ca (the ongoing c- with its vowel) + nu- 'I' + biyh. Vꜩ bala 'very well', the house rendering. at valib ca nu tao 'you are my daughter-in-law, so I hear': ca nu tao, ca + nu- 'I' + ta 'hear' + -o, as in the last part. She takes Xquic at her word and puts it to the test.

sentences.t: Vhat bala, ha cama quecha vi chi qui veeh; ha hacha hun chi nima cat; chi petic, at na cu valib ca nu tao,” xuꜭhax cut ri capoh.
sentences.l: Go-you(?) bala, go take their-food there that they eat(?); go harvest(?) one of great net; that you-come, you now then my-daughter-in-law I-hear-it,” she-was-told then the maiden.
sentences.i: Go, then: go and fetch their food, for those who eat (?); go and gather a great netful; then come back, since you are my daughter-in-law, so I hear,” the maiden was told.
sentences.n: Vhat bala 'go, then (?)': Brasseur reads uh'at bala, 'Va donc'; vhat may be ha 'go' (below) with at 'you', and the v- is not explained (a guess; toggle by the letters, ujat). ha cama … ha hacha 'go take … go gather' is a couplet of commands: ha 'go!' as in 006 (inferred, after Brasseur); cama 'take', the kama of earlier parts; hacha 'harvest, gather', with Brasseur's 'moissonne' (inferred; hach again in ¶11). quecha 'their food': qu- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + echa 'food' (vecha 'my food' in 007); in ¶10 the same word is written queꜭha. chi qui veeh 'that they eat (?)': veeh is as written (MS chiqui veeh; Brasseur vichi qui veeh), taken as 'eat' after his 'pour ceux qui mangent' (a guess). The division ha cama quecha vi chi qui veeh; ha hacha is ours. hun chi nima cat 'one great net': cat is the carrying net (Brasseur 'filet'), with plain c here and throughout (toggle kat, the same letters as kat 'you'). chi petic 'and come': chi + pet 'come' + -ic. na cu 'now, then'.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” she-said then.
sentences.i: “Very well,” she said.
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'very well', the house rendering: Xquic accepts the task.

sentences.t: Catepuch ta xbec pa abix ꜭo vi cabix ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, hocam vbeel cumal.
sentences.l: Then-also when she-went to field there-is there their-field the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, cleared(?) its-road by-them.
sentences.i: Then she went to the field where the maize field of Hunbatz and Hunchouen lay; its road had been cleared (?) by them.
sentences.n: Catepuch 'then also' (cate + puch written as one word; MS plain c, Brasseur Qate-; toggle K'atepuch, as in earlier parts). xbec 'she went': x- + be 'go' + -c, as in the last part. abix is the maize field, the milpa (Brasseur 'le champ'; toggle ab'ix). ꜭo vi cabix 'where their field was' (a blot lies over vi; read with Brasseur's qo vi): cabix is c- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + abix (Brasseur c'abix; toggle kab'ix). hocam is not otherwise known; 'cleared' is from Brasseur ('le chemin avait été ouvert et nettoyé par eux'), a guess; the toggle respells the letters. vbeel 'its road' (v- + be 'road' + -el). cumal 'by them'.

sentences.t: Xu taqueh cut capoh, xopon puch chi ri pa abix.
sentences.l: She-followed-it then maiden, she-arrived-there also at the in field.
sentences.i: The maiden followed it, and she came there, to the field.
sentences.n: Xu taqueh 'she followed it': x- + v- 'she' + taqueh 'follow' (inferred, as in 010; Brasseur takeh). xopon 'she arrived there' (opon, arriving away from the speaker). chi ri pa abix 'there, in the field': Brasseur prints chiri 'there' as one word.

sentences.t: Xa cu huvi ri abix; xma ꜭo chivi vcavi, roxvi; xu vachelaam vi vvach chi huvi.
sentences.l: Only then one-head the field; there-was-not any-more(?) its-second-head, its-third-head; it-bore-fruit(?) there its-fruit at one-head.
sentences.i: But the field was only a single plant; there was no second, no third; it bore its fruit (?) on a single stalk.
sentences.n: huvi 'one head': hun 'one' + vi 'head, top' (the vi of chuvi 'on top of'; toggle juwi'), here a single maize plant. vcavi, roxvi 'a second head, a third head': v- 'its' + ca (as in caib 'two') + vi, and r- + ox 'three' + vi (Brasseur u ca-vi r'ox-vi); Brasseur renders 'qu'une seule gerbe; car il n'en restait ni deux, ni trois'. Each huvi carries a raised t-like mark over the vi, taken as Ximénez's heavy accent, which he puts on most final vi here; in the second huvi the manuscript has u where Brasseur prints havi. chivi is taken as chi 'any more' + vi, written as one word (inferred; toggle by the letters). xma ꜭo 'there was not'. vachelaam is not otherwise known; it is built on vach 'face, fruit', and 'bore fruit' is a guess (Brasseur 'une seule gerbe sortant encore son image'); the toggle respells the letters.

sentences.t: Ta xquiz cut vꜭux ri capoh: “Quila in macol, in ꜭazbol! Apa xchin cam vi ri hun cat echa ca bixic?” xcha cut.
sentences.l: Then it-ended then her-heart the maiden: “Alas(?) I sinner, I debtor(?)! Where shall-I take there the one net food it-is-said?” she-said then.
sentences.i: Then the maiden's heart failed her: “Alas (?), I am a sinner, I am a debtor (?)! Where shall I get the net of food that was spoken of?” she said.
sentences.n: xquiz cut vꜭux 'her heart came to an end': xquiz 'it finished' (toggle xk'is), the heart giving out in despair (Brasseur 'le cœur de la jeune fille se brisa'). Quila is not otherwise known; 'alas' is a guess from the cry that follows (toggle by the letters, kila). in macol, in ꜭazbol is a couplet: macol 'sinner', mac 'sin' + -ol, the agent ending (Brasseur 'Malheureuse pécheresse que je suis!'); ꜭazbol (the g-shaped letter, read ꜭ; Brasseur qazbol) is taken as 'debtor', ꜭaz 'debt' + -bol, not the ꜭaz 'live' of ꜭazlic (a guess). Apa xchin cam vi 'where shall I take it from': xchin 'I shall', cam 'take' (Brasseur qam; toggle k'am, as in 006). hun cat echa 'one net of food'. ca bixic 'it is said, spoken of' (bih 'say' + passive), as in the last part. xcha cut: the manuscript writes plain ch in this one tag, where every other tag in the part has ꜭh (xꜭha); it is printed as written, as 006's cha cut (toggle xcha).

sentences.t: Catepuch vziquixic Chahal Echa rumal: “Ta hul val oc, ta hul tacal oc.
sentences.l: Then-also his-being-called Guardian Food by-her: “Let come(?) val(?) (oc), let come(?) alighting (oc).
sentences.i: Then the Guardian of Food was called upon by her: “Let it come (?), let it come and settle (?).
sentences.n: vziquixic 'his being called upon': v- + ziquij 'call' + passive -x + -ic (as xziquinic 'he called' in an earlier part; toggle usik'ixik); rumal 'by her'. Chahal Echa 'the Guardian of Food' (chahal 'guardian', echa 'food'), capitalised as the name of the one she calls on; Brasseur 'le Gardien des aliments'. A blot lies over the final l of Chahal (read with Brasseur). Ta hul val oc, ta hul tacal oc is a doubtful reading (MS tahul vatloc tahul tacaloc): after va the hand has a tall crossed stroke and then l, read as Ximénez's crossed double l (as in rall, vall), so val oc, parallel to tacal oc; it may instead be va vloc, which is how Brasseur seems to read it. ta 'let'; hul is taken with Brasseur as ul 'come' written with h (a guess; toggle by the letters, the same letters as jul 'hollow'); tacal 'alighting, coming to rest', as in earlier parts (inferred). What val means here is not known. Brasseur takes these words as narrative: 'afin d'obtenir qu'il en rapportât'.

sentences.t: Xtoh, Xcanil, Xcacau, ix pu ꜩiya; at Chahal re queꜭha Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen!” xꜭha ri capoh.
sentences.l: Xtoh, Xcanil, Xcacau, you also tziya(?); you Guardian of their-food Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen!” she-said the maiden.
sentences.i: Xtoh, Xcanil, Xcacau, and you who cook the maize (?); you, Guardian of the food of Hunbatz and Hunchouen!” said the maiden.
sentences.n: Xtoh, Xcanil, Xcacau are names (capitalised by us), kept in the English. Brasseur's note takes them as 'trois divinités qui présidaient à la nourriture, à l'abondance', each a goddess, each name with x (ix) 'woman': Xtoh from toh, a day of the calendar which the authors render 'rain'; Xcanil from ganil, from gan 'yellow', ripeness, the goddess of harvests (he prints Xganil in his K'iche' and Xcanil in his French; the manuscript has plain c); Xcacau from cacau 'cacao' (he prints Xcacou). The toggle respells the letters (Xtoj, Xkanil, Xkakaw). ix pu ꜩiya 'you also, ꜩiya': ix 'you (pl.)'; Brasseur's note says ꜩiya in its ordinary sense is to cook maize with ash or potash, and he renders 'vous qui préparez le maïs avec la cendre' (inferred; toggle tziya). at Chahal re queꜭha 'you, guardian of their food': re 'of'; queꜭha is the quecha of ¶7, here written with gh (ꜭh) where ¶7 has plain ch (Brasseur qu'echa both times); printed as written, and the toggle follows each spelling (kech'a, kecha), as the last part's ahuꜭhan / ahuchan.

sentences.t: Ta xu cam cut ri zamiy, vzamiyal vvi hal; xu boc acan oc; maui xu hach ri hal;
sentences.l: Then she-took then the silk(?), its-silk(?) its-top ear; she-pulled-it(?) up (oc); not she-harvested(?) the ear;
sentences.i: Then she took the silk, the silk at the top of the ear; she drew it upward (?), but she did not pick the ear;
sentences.n: xu cam 'she took' (cam 'take'; Brasseur qam; toggle k'am, as in ¶9). ri zamiy, vzamiyal vvi hal 'the silk, the silk of the top of the ear' is read with Brasseur's 'les barbes et l'extrémité de la gerbe' (inferred): zamiy has plain z (no ascender; Brasseur tzamiy, u tzamiyal), and vzamiyal is the same word with v- 'its' and -al; the toggle respells the letters (samiy, usamiyal). vvi 'its top', the vi 'head, top' of ¶9 (toggle uwi'). hal is taken as the ear of maize (Brasseur 'gerbe'; toggle jal, the same letters as jal 'change'). xu boc acan oc 'she pulled it upward': boc is not otherwise known, and 'pull' is from Brasseur's 'les arracha doucement' (inferred; toggle b'ok); acan oc 'upward' (acan 'climb'). maui xu hach ri hal 'she did not harvest the ear': hach is the root of hacha in ¶7 (Brasseur 'sans déraciner la gerbe').

sentences.t: chi cau cut ri hal echa pa cat; xcaxinic ri nima cat.
sentences.l: that cau(?) then the ear food in net; it-was-filled(?) the great net.
sentences.i: and the ears of food were laid (?) in the net, and the great net was filled (?).
sentences.n: chi cau: the letter is u (joined at the bottom), not n (Brasseur chi cau). cau is not otherwise known; Brasseur renders the clause 'les arrangea (ces barbes devenant des) gerbes de maïs au fond du filet', and 'laid' is a guess along his lines. hal echa 'ears of food': the silk has become ears. xcaxinic is not otherwise known; 'it was filled' follows Brasseur ('elle réussit ainsi à remplir un grand filet'), a guess; the toggle respells the letters. At the start of the manuscript line, before cat, a struck letter with a blot is not printed.

sentences.t: Ta xpe cut ri capoh. Xa cu chicop xecan ri cat.
sentences.l: Then she-came then the maiden. Only then animals carried the net.
sentences.i: Then the maiden came away. It was animals that carried the net.
sentences.n: xpe 'she came' (pe 'come'). Xa cu chicop xecan 'only animals carried it': chicop 'animal'; xecan is taken as xe- (they, completed) + ecan 'carry a load', the vowels run together (recan 'her load' below; Brasseur x-ekan, his k standing for q; inferred, and the toggle keeps k, xekan, as 012 did for ahchoce). Brasseur's note on chicop: the word means any beast, but is also used of a brutish, uncivilised man; Ximénez translates 'animal', and Brasseur prefers 'barbares'. The English follows Ximénez's 'animal'.

sentences.t: Ta xpetic, xbe qui ya vcoc xucut ha, quehe ri recan.
sentences.l: When she-came, went they-put-it its-going-in(?) side house, thus the her-load.
sentences.i: When she came, they went and set it inside (?), in the corner of the house, as if it were her load (?).
sentences.n: xpetic 'she came' (pet 'come' + -ic). xbe qui ya 'they went and put it': xbe 'went', qui- 'they' + ya 'give, put'. vcoc is taken as 'its going in', with oc 'enter', as in 006 (inferred; Brasseur u coc). xucut ha 'the side of the house, its corner': xucut 'side', as in an earlier part, and ha 'house' (MS xucutha, divided with Brasseur). quehe ri recan 'just so, her load': recan, r- 'her' + ecan 'load, burden' (Brasseur r'ekan, 'comme leur fardeau (ordinaire)'); taken as 'as if she had carried it herself', a guess.

sentences.t: Xoponic, xril ri atit. Catepuch ta xril ri atit ri echa hun chi nima cat:
sentences.l: She-arrived, she-saw-her the grandmother. Then-also when she-saw-it the grandmother the food one of great net:
sentences.i: She arrived, and the grandmother saw her; and when the grandmother saw the food, a whole great netful:
sentences.n: Xoponic 'she arrived' (opon + -ic, the ending at the end of a clause). xril 'she saw her, she saw it': x- + r- (the form before a vowel) + il 'see'. The two clauses repeat xril ri atit, first of the maiden, then of the food. ri echa hun chi nima cat 'the food, one great net', the words of the grandmother's command in ¶7. The colon leads into her speech.

sentences.t: “Apa mi xpe vi ri echa auumal? Mi xe a calaba vi, ve mi xquiz a cam vloc ri cabix?
sentences.l: “Where just-now it-came there the food by-you(?)? Just-now them you calaba(?) there, or just-now finished your taking hither the our-field?
sentences.i: “Where has this food of yours come from? Have you laid it waste (?), or have you carried off all of our field?
sentences.n: Apa mi xpe vi 'where has it come from': mi 'just now' + xpe 'it came', with vi pointing back to apa. auumal is a doubtful reading (MS a u u mal, three minim groups before m; Brasseur aumal), printed as written as one word: it is taken as a- 'you' + umal, as in rumal 'by him' and cumal 'by them', with v (written u) before the vowel, 'by you, of yours' (inferred; toggle awumal). Mi xe a calaba vi 'have you calaba-ed them': xe, x- + e 'them'; a- 'you'; calaba is not otherwise known and doubtful: between a and calaba the hand has a tall l-like stroke, not the 3-shaped tresillo, taken as a false start and not printed, and the c is printed plain; Brasseur reads galaba, his g standing for ꜫ, which would make it ꜫalaba. 'Laid waste' follows his 'aurais-tu donc ruiné (mon champ)', a guess; the toggle respells the letters. ve 'or, whether'. xquiz a cam vloc 'have you finished carrying it here': xquiz 'it finished', a cam 'your taking' (Brasseur qam; toggle k'am). ri cabix 'our field': here ca- 'our' + abix (Brasseur k'abix, his k standing for q; toggle qab'ix), where in ¶8 the same letters were 'their field' (kab'ix), as 010's cochoch was both 'their home' and 'our home'.

sentences.t: Chi be na vila,” xꜭha ri atit.
sentences.l: That go now I-see-it,” she-said the grandmother.
sentences.i: Let me go now and see it,” said the grandmother.
sentences.n: Chi be na vila 'let (me) go first and see it': chi, the optative 'let'; be 'go'; na 'first, now'; vila 'I see it', v- 'I' + il + -a, as in the last part (Brasseur 'Je vais y voir à l'instant').

sentences.t: Ta xbe puch, xbe rila ri abix.
sentences.l: Then she-went also, she-went she-sees-it the field.
sentences.i: And she went; she went to look at the field.
sentences.n: xbe … xbe 'she went … she went': the verb doubled. rila 'she sees it': r- (the form before a vowel) + il + -a; the r is shaped like a v in the manuscript (Brasseur x-be r'ila).

sentences.t: Xavi xere ꜭo vi ri huvi abix; xavi cu xere calah vcolibal cat chuxe.
sentences.l: Just so there-is there the one-head field; just then so clear its-lying-place(?) net at-its-foot.
sentences.i: The single plant of the field was still standing there, just as before; and just as plain, at its foot, was the place where the net had lain.
sentences.n: A couplet: xavi xere … xavi cu xere 'just so … just so, then'. ꜭo vi 'is there' (the g-shaped letter, read ꜭ). huvi abix 'the one plant of the field', as in ¶9. calah 'clear, plain to see' (toggle q'alaj). vcolibal: v- 'its' + col + -ibal, the ending of place; Brasseur reads u qolibal ('l'endroit où avait été placé le filet'), with his q for ꜭ, which would make it the ꜭol 'lie, be placed' of ¶1's xꜭol oc. The manuscript has plain c, and the toggle respells the letters (ukolib'al; compare 006's vcolbal 'his means of saving', from col 'save'). 'The place where the net had lain' follows Brasseur (inferred). chuxe 'at its foot' (chi + v- + xe 'root, foot').

sentences.t: Anim chicut xpe ri atit, xul chicut chi rochoch;
sentences.l: Quickly again-then she-came the grandmother, she-arrived again-then at her-home;
sentences.i: Quickly the grandmother came back and arrived again at her home,
sentences.n: anim 'quickly'. xpe … xul 'she came … she arrived here', with chicut 'again, then' in both clauses. chi rochoch 'at her home' (MS chirochoch): r- 'her' + ochoch 'home'.

sentences.t: xꜭha chicut chire ri capoh: “Xere vi retal ri quiꜩih vi chi at valib.
sentences.l: she-said again-then to-her the maiden: “Thus there its-sign the truly there that you my-daughter-in-law.
sentences.i: and she said to the maiden: “This is the sign that truly you are my daughter-in-law.
sentences.n: Xere vi retal 'just this is the sign': retal, r- 'its' + etal 'sign', the etal of quetal in ¶3 (Brasseur 'C'est là véritablement un signe'). quiꜩih vi chi at valib 'that truly you are my daughter-in-law' takes up Xquic's own words in ¶4, quiꜩih vi chi in alib la.

sentences.t: Chi vil chi na a banoh, ri e ꜭo ri vi e nauinac chic,” xuꜭhax cut capoh.
sentences.l: That I-see still now your-doing, the they there-are the vi(?) they wise(?) already,” she-was-told then maiden.
sentences.i: I shall see yet what you do, and those who are there (?), who are wise already (?),” the maiden was told.
sentences.n: Chi vil 'let me see it': chi + v- 'I' + il 'see'. chi na 'still, yet'. a banoh 'your doing, your deeds' (ban 'do' + -oh). ri e ꜭo ri vi e nauinac chic is a doubtful division (MS riegorivi enauinac | chic; divided with Brasseur's ri e qo ri vienauinakchie): ri e ꜭo 'those who are there' are perhaps the children she carries (Brasseur 'celles des sages que tu portes (actuellement dans ton sein)'); the sense of ri vi is unclear, and it is left out of the English. nauinac is taken as nao 'know' (as in ahnaoh 'thinker' in 009) + -inac, the state reached, 'those who have come to know, the wise' (inferred; toggle nawinaq). With xuꜭhax cut capoh 'the maiden was told' the part ends at Ximénez's own heading: the next line announces the birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
